sub_topics: CJP has been peppered with questions on SC decision on DAP (Araullo v. Aquino, July 1, 2014)
Q1: By filing MR, does government expect SC to reverse its unanimous 13-0 decision?
As private citizen, CJP cannot speak for government
However, MR is filed not necessarily to reverse a decision
In fact, CJP doesn't think justices will completely turn it around
But they can modify or clarify it
Q2: PNoy complained decision 'put our country's development in a state of paralysis' -- do you agree?
With due respect, CJP would rather look at the bright side
True, SC declared unconstitutional some 'acts and practices under the DAP' -- dark side, bad news PNoy is referring to
But bright side, good news: 'doctrine of operative fact is applicable to the adoption and implementation of the DAP' (p87, decision)
Simply means actions and programs done prior to declaration of unconstitutionality are valid and enforceable
Unconstitutionality has a prospective effect -- only future 'acts and practices' would be adversely affected
Thus, bridges, roads and schoolhouses built with DAP funds need not be destroyed
Those given to BSP to increase its capital, or transferred to House for 'construction of Legislative Library and Archives Building' (cross-border transfer) need not be returned
Decision (p21) states 'DAP as a program had been meanwhile discontinued because it had fully served its purpose'
Implies DAP no longer needed to stimulate economy since funds for such purpose had been amply provided for in 2013 budget

Q3: PNoy's argument that decision condemned officials without due process -- p.90 said operative-fact doctrine 'cannot apply to the authors, proponents and implementors of the DAP, unless there are concrete findings of good faith in their favor by the proper tribunals determining their criminal, civil, administrative and other liabilities'
That quotation appears alien to otherwise well-crafted and balanced decision penned by Justice Lucas P. Bersamin
As PNoy pointed out, contradicts constitutional presumption of innocence, of good faith and of regularity in the performance of official duties
But all is not lost. In ruling on MR, Court could delete this from decision, or clarify it to assure no prejudgment of liability
Or explain statement is merely nonbinding obiter dictum (side comment) not supported by fallo or dispositive portion
Q4: Why decision's fallo says only some 'acts and practices under DAP' are unconstitutional; why not DAP itself?
As stressed in CJP's July 6 column (A407), Araullo v. Aquino did not strike down DAP itself, only some 'acts and practices' under it
Unlike Belgica v. Ochoa (Nov 13, 2013) which plainly declared PDAF unconstitutional
Reason: DAP is just sophisticated name for power of augmentation granted by Charter not only to President but also to SP, Speaker, CJ, and heads of independent constitutional commissions
To transfer funds from one budget item to another budget item
Being merely an exception to constitutional ban on 'transfers of appropriations,' this power has strict limitations
Transfers may be made only from one item to another item in the same branch or office
Cross-border transfers are prohibited
Thus President cannot transfer savings from executive item to deficient item in legislature or judiciary
Parallel: Charter gives President power of appointment, but subject to limitations
Constitution says only Filipinos may be named judges
If President appoints alien to judiciary, that 'act' would be unconstitutional but not the power to appoint
Neither are other appointments which observed limitations affected
Likewise, augmentation made without observing limitations would be unconstitutional, but power to augment itself would not be
Other augmentations which observed limitations would not be affected
Decision went further: under operative-fact doctrine, only future unconstitutional augmentations would be deemed void and unenforceable
Q5: Can PNoy use DAP again in the future?
Yes, nothing prevents the President from transferring funds from one item to another provided he observes constitutional limitations
DAP just another name for power of augmentation, not itself unconstitutional
Only some 'acts and practices under it' were unconstitutional
PNoy can ask Congress to pass supplemental budget
Or to redefine 'savings'
Or to refine the law requiring certification from national treasurer to use unprogrammed funds

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban opens his two-part DAP Q&A series with questions Q1-Q5; the remaining four (Q6-Q9) follow next Sunday in A404. CJ has been peppered with questions on the SC decision on the Disbursement Acceleration Program or DAP (Araullo v. Aquino, July 1, 2014). Q1: By filing an MR, does the government expect the SC to reverse its unanimous 13-0 decision? As a private citizen, CJ cannot speak for the government; however, an MR is filed not necessarily to reverse a decision -- in fact, CJ does not think the justices will completely turn it around, but they can modify or clarify it. Q2: The President complained that the decision 'put our country's development in a state of paralysis' -- do you agree? With due respect, CJ would rather look at the bright side. True, the SC declared unconstitutional some 'acts and practices under the DAP' -- the dark side, the bad news PNoy is referring to. But the bright side, the good news, is that the 'doctrine of operative fact is applicable to the adoption and implementation of the DAP' (p.87) -- this simply means actions and programs done prior to the declaration of unconstitutionality are valid and enforceable; in short, unconstitutionality has a prospective effect: only future 'acts and practices' would be adversely affected. Thus, bridges, roads, and schoolhouses built with DAP funds need not be destroyed, and those given to the BSP to increase its capital, or transferred to the House of Representatives (a 'cross-border transfer') for the 'construction of the Legislative Library and Archives Building' need not be returned. So, too, the decision (p.21) states that 'the DAP as a program had been meanwhile discontinued because it had fully served its purpose' -- implying that the DAP is no longer needed to stimulate the economy since the funds for such purpose had been amply provided for in the 2013 budget. Q3: Please comment on PNoy's argument that the decision condemned government officials without due process when, on p.90, it said that the operative-fact doctrine 'cannot apply to the authors, proponents and implementors of the DAP, unless there are concrete findings of good faith in their favor by the proper tribunals determining their criminal, civil, administrative and other liabilities.' That quotation appears alien to the otherwise well-crafted and balanced decision penned by Justice Lucas P. Bersamin. As PNoy pointed out, it contradicts the constitutional presumption of innocence, of good faith and of the regularity in the performance of official duties. But all is not lost -- in its ruling on the government's MR, the Court could delete this from its decision, or clarify it to assure that this is not a prejudgment of liability and that no one shall be condemned or penalized without due process, as ordained by the Constitution; it could also explain that this statement is merely a non-binding obiter dictum (side comment) not supported by its fallo or dispositive portion. Q4: Why did the decision's fallo say that only some 'acts and practices under the DAP' are unconstitutional; why not the DAP itself? As stressed in CJ's July 6 column (A407), Araullo v. Aquino did not strike down the DAP itself, only some 'acts and practices' under it, unlike Belgica v. Ochoa (Nov 13, 2013), which plainly declared the PDAF unconstitutional. The reason is that the DAP is just a sophisticated name for the power of augmentation granted by the Charter not only to the President but also to the Senate President, House Speaker, CJ, and heads of independent constitutional commissions, to transfer funds from one budget item to another budget item. Being merely an exception to the constitutional ban on 'transfers of appropriations,' this power has strict limitations -- for instance, transfers may be made only from one item to another item in the same branch or office; cross-border transfers are prohibited; thus, the President cannot transfer savings from a budget item in the executive branch to a deficient budget item in the legislature, or in the judiciary. CJ cites a parallel: the Charter gives the President the power of appointment, however, such power is subject to limitations; example: the Constitution says that only Filipinos may be named judges, so if the President appoints an alien to the judiciary, that 'act' would be unconstitutional but not the power to appoint, neither are the other appointments which observed the limitations. Likewise, an augmentation made without observing the limitations would be unconstitutional, but the power to augment itself would not be; also, other augmentations which observed the limitations would not be affected; in fact, the decision went further by saying that, under the operative-fact doctrine, only future unconstitutional augmentations would be deemed void and unenforceable. Q5: Can the President use the DAP again in the future? Yes, nothing prevents the President from transferring funds from one item to another provided he observes the constitutional limitations pointed out in the decision; to stress, the DAP, which is just another name for the power of augmentation, is not itself unconstitutional -- only some 'acts and practices under it.' Also, he can ask Congress to pass a supplemental budget, or to redefine 'savings,' or to refine the law requiring a certification from the national treasurer to use unprogrammed funds.
